ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: The figure divides the isomers of hexane into three classes according to the degree of branching of the carbon skeleton. The bracket on the left is labeled I, and the structure inside is the most branched and can be regarded as a highly branched hexane isomer; the bracket on the right is labeled II, and the structure inside has one branch, with a medium degree of branching; the bracket in the middle is labeled III, and inside is a longer continuous zigzag carbon chain, with the least branching or no branching. Reasoning: The question states that these are all hexane isomers, so the molecular formulas are the same and the molecular weights are basically the same. For alkane isomers, the more branching, the smaller the molecular surface area, the weaker the intermolecular dispersion forces, and the lower the boiling point; the less branching, the higher the boiling point. Therefore the least-branched III has the highest boiling point, the moderately branched II is next, and the most-branched I is lowest. The order is III > II > I.

method.method_draft: First describe the image: identify the three classes I, II, and III and compare how branched their carbon skeletons are. Then use the text statement that all are isomers of hexane, so they have the same formula and comparable molecular mass. Apply the rule that among alkane isomers, boiling point decreases as branching increases. Therefore the least-branched class III has the highest boiling point, class II is intermediate, and the most-branched class I is lowest: III > II > I.
